::: {.callout-note title="Chapter overview"}
An additive straight-line model gives each predictor one partial slope.
This chapter asks when a comparison should instead vary across another
predictor's values or groups. A product term makes that possibility
explicit. We follow its meaning from generated practice-and-preparation
records to faculty salaries and conformity responses: interpret the
coefficients at their anchors, estimate conditional comparisons, show
where the records support them, and evaluate their uncertainty. By the end,
you can distinguish a varying association from a causal explanation and
write an informative report even when the slopes are poorly distinguished.
:::

The same equation can pose different research questions. An extra hour
of practice may have different associations with achievement at different
preparation levels. A year's service may have different salary associations
across academic ranks. We begin with the comparison that an additive model
holds fixed, then examine what changes when it is allowed to vary.

## A Comparison That Depends on Another Predictor {#ch10-question}


### The restriction the additive model imposes

Suppose a researcher asks whether students who spend more time in
deliberate practice tend to achieve higher posttest scores. An additive
regression can allow students with stronger prior preparation to have
higher scores while requiring the practice-score relationship to be the
same at every preparation level. That requirement may be the very claim
the researcher needs to examine. Perhaps an additional hour of practice
is associated with a small score difference for students with lower
prior preparation and a larger difference for students with higher
prior preparation. Or perhaps the apparent difference is only sampling
noise.

The central question is therefore conditional:

> How does the expected outcome difference associated with one unit of a
> focal predictor vary across meaningful values or groups of another
> predictor?

An **interaction** is the model term that permits such variation. On the
modeled scale, interaction means departure from additivity. Parallel
lines are additive; nonparallel lines are interactive. The lines need
not cross inside the observed data, and a statistically detectable
product term does not by itself identify a causal mechanism.



::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}

Arrows compare two with four practice hours at baseline 60 and 80: both differences are 5 under additivity, versus 2.6 and 7.4 under interaction. These are conditional model means.](chapter_10_files/figure-html/fig-ch10-additive-interactive-1.png){#fig-ch10-additive-interactive fig-pos='H' fig-alt='Two panels show expected score against practice. Additive lines at baseline 60 and 80 have equal two-hour differences of 5. Interactive lines have two-hour differences of 2.6 and 7.4, shown by arrows. The lines do not cross.' width=604.8}

Read the arrows as conditional comparisons. In the interactive panel,
two additional practice hours correspond to 2.6 score points at baseline
60 and 7.4 at baseline 80. Their difference is 4.8 points. The product
term will express this changing comparison in one equation. The lines
are model means at two named baseline values: they are neither individual
students' trajectories nor separate regressions fitted after splitting
the students into groups. Section 2.4 declares this model and generates
one sample from it.

This chapter first uses a simulation in which the conditional
relationship is known. It then studies a real observational example:
nine-month salary, years of service, and academic rank for the faculty
of one U.S. college in 2008-09, from the package-distributed
`carData::Salaries` data. The two examples play different roles. The
simulation verifies algebra and repeated-sample logic against known
truth. The salary analysis forces the harder decisions about units,
severely unequal support, factor coding, uncertainty, diagnostics, and
bounded reporting — and it shows what an honest interaction report looks
like when the data do not clearly distinguish rank-specific slopes from
one common slope.


### The same idea for groups and continuous predictors

Chapter 4's factorial model allowed the practice-schedule difference to
vary across feedback groups: its interaction test gave $F(2,18)=9.6$,
$p=.0015$, and its declared difference of differences was 4 with SE 1.8257.
Chapter 6 fitted that model in R. Here a continuous predictor replaces one
factor, so a surface replaces a finite cell table and a moving slope
replaces a single difference of differences. The ANOVA foundations remain
the same; what changes is the form of the conditional comparison.

### Interaction is defined on a stated scale

Additivity is always defined on a scale. Lines that are nonparallel for
salary in dollars remain nonparallel after converting dollars to
thousands of dollars, although every outcome coefficient is divided by
1,000. A
nonlinear transformation such as a logarithm can change whether a
pattern appears additive because it changes the model itself, not merely
the label on the axis.

The same caution matters in later generalized linear models: interaction
on a linear-predictor scale need not look the same on a response scale.
This chapter stays with continuous outcomes and the identity-link linear
model. Logistic interaction, multilevel interaction, and three-way
interaction are outside its worked scope.

::: {.callout-warning title="Moderation is not mediation or mechanism"}
A moderator names where a focal relationship is allowed to vary. That
reading describes when an association differs, rather than how an effect
is transmitted. An intervening variable and a causal mechanism need
additional design and identification evidence. Chapter 14 develops those
requirements.
:::

## The Product Term and Its Coefficients {#ch10-product}


### The product coefficient is a difference in slopes

Begin with two continuous predictors, $X$ and $W$, and a continuous
outcome, $Y$. An additive conditional-mean model is

$$
E(Y_i\mid X_i,W_i)=\beta_0+\beta_X X_i+\beta_W W_i.
$$

Holding $W$ fixed, the expected difference associated with a one-unit
difference in $X$ is always $\beta_X$. Holding $X$ fixed, the expected
difference associated with a one-unit difference in $W$ is always
$\beta_W$. The model permits different levels but not different slopes.

The product-term model is

$$
E(Y_i\mid X_i,W_i)
=\beta_0+\beta_X X_i+\beta_W W_i+\beta_{XW}X_iW_i.
$$ {#eq-continuous-interaction}

Regrouping the terms that involve $X$ gives

$$
E(Y_i\mid X_i,W_i)
=\left(\beta_0+\beta_W W_i\right)
 + \left(\beta_X+\beta_{XW}W_i\right)X_i.
$$

The conditional slope of $X$ at $W=w$ is therefore

$$
\frac{\partial E(Y\mid X,W)}{\partial X}
=\beta_X+\beta_{XW}w.
$$ {#eq-conditional-slope-x}

If $\beta_{XW}=0$, the slope does not vary with $W$ and the model is
additive. If $\beta_{XW}\ne0$, a one-unit difference in $W$ changes the
conditional slope of $X$ by $\beta_{XW}$. This is what the product
coefficient measures. It is a **difference in slopes**, not the slope of
$X$ at every value of $W$.

The same model can be regrouped around $W$:

$$
\frac{\partial E(Y\mid X,W)}{\partial W}
=\beta_W+\beta_{XW}x.
$$ {#eq-conditional-slope-w}

The algebra is symmetric: each predictor's conditional slope depends on
the other. Substantive language need not be symmetric. Researchers often
call $W$ a **moderator** when theory makes $X$ the focal predictor and
$W$ the variable across which the $X$ relationship is expected to vary;
the conditional slope $\beta_X+\beta_{XW}w$ is then called a **simple
slope** or conditional effect at $w$ [@aiken1991; @hayes2022]. That label
comes from the research question, not from a privileged side of the
multiplication sign.

For two values $x_a$ and $x_b$ at the same moderator value $w$, the
conditional mean contrast is

$$
E(Y\mid x_b,w)-E(Y\mid x_a,w)
=(x_b-x_a)\left(\beta_X+\beta_{XW}w\right).
$$

That sentence contains several safeguards:

- it identifies the outcome scale;
- it identifies the focal predictor difference;
- it holds the other predictor at a stated value;
- it describes a conditional mean, not every case; and
- it remains associational unless the research design supports a causal
  interpretation.


### Hierarchy: the lower-order terms stay

The formula

```r
y ~ x * w
```

expands to `x + w + x:w`. The lower-order terms belong with their
product term. This **hierarchy principle** has both mathematical and
interpretive reasons [@cohen2003; @kutner2005].

First, deleting $X$ while retaining $XW$ constrains the slope of $X$ to
zero when $W=0$. Deleting $W$ imposes the analogous constraint at
$X=0$. Such constraints are rarely part of the research question.
Second, shifting either predictor changes which lower-order coefficients
represent slopes and differences. A hierarchical model remains the same
fitted surface after a change of origin; a product-only model generally
does not. Third, factor product terms are often represented by several
columns, so retaining the full lower-order structure keeps the block's
meaning coherent.

Hierarchy does not mean every possible product must be added. The
interaction should be motivated by the research question, graph, design,
or a prespecified model comparison. It means that once a product is in
the model, its component terms remain.


### Centering changes the question at zero

Let $W_c=W-c$. Substituting $W=W_c+c$ into
@eq-continuous-interaction gives

$$
E(Y\mid X,W_c)
=(\beta_0+c\beta_W)
 +(\beta_X+c\beta_{XW})X
 +\beta_WW_c+\beta_{XW}XW_c.
$$

Centering $W$ at $c$ therefore changes the intercept and the
lower-order coefficient of $X$. The new $X$ coefficient is the
conditional slope at the original value $W=c$. It does not change the
interaction coefficient, fitted values, residuals, or the corresponding
full-versus-reduced product-block test. Centering is a
**reparameterization**: it puts zero at a value that makes a coefficient
worth interpreting [@aiken1991].

Centering is not a remedy for confounding, selection bias, measurement
error, omitted nonlinearity, lack of overlap, or a poorly specified
research question. It can change correlations among constructed columns
and may make numerical output easier to read, but it does not add
information or make unsupported comparisons valid.

Scaling is another reparameterization. If $X_{10}=X/10$, then a one-unit
difference in $X_{10}$ is a ten-unit difference in $X$. Coefficients and
standard errors change units together; fitted values and substantive
conclusions should agree after correct translation.


### A known-truth example: what one sample recovers

Consider a deliberately simplified educational setting. Each row is one
student. The focal predictor is weekly deliberate practice in hours,
$X$. The second predictor is a baseline assessment score, $W$. The
outcome is a posttest score, $Y$. The simulation asks an associational
model question under known conditions: how does the practice-score slope
vary with baseline score?

The data-generating process centers baseline score at 70:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_i={}&60+2.5X_i+0.4(W_i-70)\\
 &+0.12X_i(W_i-70)+\varepsilon_i,\\
\varepsilon_i&\sim\mathcal N(0,5^2).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-simulation-dgp}

The coefficients are fixed by design. At a baseline score of 70, the
true practice slope is 2.5 score points per hour. Ten baseline points
below that anchor, it is
$2.5+0.12(-10)=1.3$ points per hour. Ten points above, it is
$2.5+0.12(10)=3.7$ points per hour. The positive product coefficient
does not say that practice changes baseline preparation, or vice versa;
it says that the conditional mean surface is nonadditive.

Practice hours and baseline scores are generated independently here so
that the interaction mechanics are transparent. Real educational data
would demand attention to attendance, access to support, prior courses,
measurement reliability, clustering within classrooms or schools, and
the process by which practice time was chosen. None of those design
complications is solved by fitting a product term.


The explicit seed makes this one sample reproducible. It does not make
the sample representative of a real population. The observed baseline
range is 42.8747 to
96, and practice lies between
0.0141 and
7.9802 hours. Conditional estimates
outside this rectangle would be extrapolations even though the generating
equation is known to us.

The working object `sim` holds `score`, `hours`, `base` and
`baseline_c = base - 70`. Generating the baseline, practice and independent
error in that order with seed 909 gives the declared sample.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(909)
base <- pmin(pmax(rnorm(320, 70, 10), 42), 96)
hours <- runif(320, 0, 8)
baseline_c <- base - 70
score <- 60 + 2.5*hours + .4*baseline_c +
  .12*hours*baseline_c + rnorm(320, 0, 5)
sim <- data.frame(score, hours, base, baseline_c)
m1 <- lm(score ~ hours * baseline_c, data = sim)
```
:::

2.6972 points per
hour, compared with the true value 2.5. The fitted interaction is

[0.0875,

The fitted lower-order coefficient for centered baseline,
0.3822, is the baseline
score slope when practice is zero. It is not a baseline-score slope
averaged over all practice values. In an interaction model, every
lower-order coefficient is conditional on the other component being at
its coded zero or reference level.


### The product block against the additive restriction

The reduced model is written first because it states the restriction
being evaluated: one common practice slope and one common baseline
slope. The full model releases the common-slope restriction by adding
the product.


The nested comparison gives

$$
F=\frac{(RSS_R-RSS_F)/q}{RSS_F/(n-p)}
=\frac{(9108.7071-7488.7866)/1}{7488.7866/316}=68.3548,
\qquad p<.0001.
$$

Here $q=1$ added coefficient and $p=4$ total coefficients. The product
coefficient's $t=8.2677$ has the same squared statistic from full precision.
Both models use the same 320 outcomes.

Here the product block has one degree of freedom because both predictors
are continuous. The comparison asks whether allowing the practice slope
to vary linearly with baseline score reduces residual variation beyond
the additive model. It does not test whether the entire model is true,
whether the relationship is causal, or whether the interaction is large
enough to matter in a particular decision.

In the one-degree-of-freedom case, the block $F$ statistic equals the
squared $t$ statistic for the product coefficient. That identity does
not generalize to a factor with three levels: a continuous-by-three-level
factor interaction requires two product columns and a joint two-degree-
of-freedom test.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m0 <- lm(score ~ hours + baseline_c, data = sim)
anova(m0, m1)
```
:::



### Recentering leaves the surface alone

The centered model uses baseline 70 as zero. A raw-score model uses the
unobserved and impossible baseline score zero as its anchor.


| Quantity | Raw-score model | Centered model |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Coefficient of practice at the coded zero | $-5.3448$ | 2.6972 |
| Lower-order baseline coefficient | 0.3822 | 0.3822 |
| Product coefficient | 0.1149 | 0.1149 |
| Product block $F$ | 68.3548 | 68.3548 |
| Maximum fitted-value difference | below $10^{-12}$ | below $10^{-12}$ |

: What centering changes and what it leaves alone. {#tbl-ch10-centering tbl-colwidths="[46,27,27]"}


The raw model's practice coefficient is the fitted practice slope at a
baseline score of zero. Its unattractive value is not evidence that the
model failed; it answers an unsupported question. After centering, the
practice coefficient answers the supported question at baseline 70.
The product coefficient and every fitted value agree to numerical
precision.

Centering can change the p-values of lower-order coefficients because it
changes the hypotheses they test. It should not change the one-degree-
of-freedom product test in this corresponding model. A lower-order
p-value becoming smaller after centering is not repaired confounding;
it is a different conditional comparison.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
raw <- lm(score ~ hours * base, data = sim)
max(abs(fitted(raw) - fitted(m1)))
```
:::



## Probe the Conditional Comparison {#ch10-probe}


### A conditional slope needs the covariance

At a centered baseline value $w$, the fitted practice slope is

$$
\widehat\beta_X(w)=\widehat\beta_X+w\widehat\beta_{XW}.
$$

Because the two estimated coefficients are correlated, its variance is
not obtained by adding their variances alone:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}\{\widehat\beta_X(w)\}
={}&\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_X)
+w^2\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_{XW})\\
&+2w\operatorname{Cov}
(\widehat\beta_X,\widehat\beta_{XW}).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-simple-slope-variance}

The conditional-slope table applies this covariance formula to three
meaningful baseline scores. Each interval uses $t_{.975,316}=1.9675$.


| Baseline score | Target slope | Fitted slope | SE | 95% lower | 95% upper |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 60 | 1.3 | 1.5484 | 0.1780 | 1.1982 | 1.8986 |
| 70 | 2.5 | 2.6972 | 0.1244 | 2.4524 | 2.9421 |
| 80 | 3.7 | 3.8461 | 0.1947 | 3.4630 | 4.2291 |

: Conditional practice slopes at three supported baseline scores, with their declared targets. {#tbl-ch10-slopes tbl-colwidths="[20,16,16,12,18,18]"}


The estimated practice association rises from
1.5484 points per hour at baseline 60
to 3.8461 points per hour at baseline
80. These are three evaluations of one fitted surface, not three
separate regressions and not evidence that students belong to three
latent types.

The `emtrends()` function in the `emmeans` package calculates these
conditional trends and their covariance-based intervals directly.


Agreement with the manual table is a computational check. The software
does not choose defensible probe values. That responsibility remains
with the analyst.

For the slope at centered baseline $w=10$, applying the variance formula
to the full-precision covariance matrix gives variance 0.0379 and
SE 0.1947. Keep the entries at their stored precision until the final
result is reported: early rounding of small covariance terms can alter
the reconstructed SE.

Omitting covariance gives 0.1865. Adding the focal SE to ten times the
product SE gives 0.2634. Neither computes the uncertainty of the fitted
linear combination. A short contrast-vector calculation includes every
needed covariance automatically:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
b <- coef(m1); V <- vcov(m1)
cvec <- c(0, 1, 0, 10)  # intercept, hours, baseline_c, product
sum(cvec * b)
sqrt(drop(cvec %*% V %*% cvec))
```
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
emmeans::emtrends(m1, ~ baseline_c, var = "hours",
  at = list(baseline_c = c(-10, 0, 10)))
```
:::



A **simple slope** fixes the moderator and reads the focal comparison
from the whole fitted model. For a two-hour comparison, multiply the
slope and both endpoints by two: the fitted differences are 3.0969 at
baseline 60 and 7.6923 at baseline 80. A different practice interval
changes that multiplier, not the fitted relationship.

Now ask the interaction question directly: how much greater is the
practice slope at 80 than at 60? Because both slopes use the same model,
the focal coefficient cancels:

$$
\widehat\beta_X(10)-\widehat\beta_X(-10)
=20\widehat\beta_{XW}=2.2977,
\qquad SE=20\,SE(\widehat\beta_{XW})=0.2779.
$$

The 95% interval is [1.7509, 2.8445]. This compares **two slopes**, whereas
each row of @tbl-ch10-slopes compares **one slope with zero**. Their
uncertainty calculations answer different questions. In general,
$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat s_2-\widehat s_1)=
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat s_2)+\operatorname{Var}(\widehat s_1)
-2\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat s_2,\widehat s_1)$.
The two slope estimates share coefficients; subtracting interval
endpoints or adding their SEs ignores that relationship.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
20 * coef(m1)["hours:baseline_c"]
20 * confint(m1)["hours:baseline_c", ]
```
:::


A large simple slope can coexist with zero interaction: both preparation
levels might have the same strong practice association. Conversely, a
changing slope can pass through zero at one baseline. Neither a test
against zero at a chosen probe nor two separate significance labels
replace a direct slope contrast [@gelman2006].

### Choosing probe values and showing where the data are

The **pick-a-point** approach — also called the analysis of simple
slopes — evaluates conditional slopes at a small set of substantively
chosen moderator values [@aiken1991; @hayes2022]. There is no rule that
these values must be the mean and one standard deviation above and below
it. Those values may be
uninterpretable, outside the data, or different across studies. Better
choices come from the measurement scale and the research question:
policy thresholds, clinically or educationally meaningful cutoffs,
prespecified percentiles, or values needed for an actual decision.

The 60, 70, and 80 probes work here because baseline score has an
interpretable unit and all three values are well supported. A complete
report also displays the moderator distribution rather than presenting
the probes as if observations were equally dense everywhere.


### The conditional-slope curve is the primary display

Three probe values are readings of one
continuous object: the fitted conditional slope
$\widehat\beta_X(w)=\widehat\beta_X+w\widehat\beta_{XW}$ with its pointwise
band, drawn over the moderator values the data actually support. That
curve, not a boundary number, is the primary display for a continuous
moderator [@bauer2005; @hayes2022]. The marked zero-crossing boundaries are explained in Section 3.4.
Their position relative to the observed support matters as much as
their numerical value in @fig-ch10-slope-curve.



::: {.cell}

the fitted slope is slightly negative — about
$-0.4191$ score points per hour — and
its band covers zero. The band leaves zero at the upper boundary,
51.284, and the slope then rises steadily to
about 5.6843 score points per hour
at the highest observed baseline score. The three pick-a-point probes are
three readings of this same curve. The band widens toward both ends
because a conditional slope evaluated far from the centering value
borrows heavily from the product coefficient, whose own uncertainty is
then multiplied by a large $w$.

Marking the boundaries on the curve also makes the support limitation visible
rather than hidden in a table: the lower boundary sits inside the shaded
panel, where no student was generated, so nothing in these data speaks to
it.


### Levels, cases and the limit of the algebra

A slope compares changes; a fitted mean describes a level. At four
practice hours and baseline 70, the fitted mean is 70.4013 with mean-response
interval [69.8644, 70.9382]. The new-case interval [60.8082, 79.9944] is
wider because it also includes individual error variance. At baselines 60
and 80, the fitted means are 61.9836 and 78.8189. Precision about a mean
does not imply precise prediction of each student.

A **Johnson-Neyman** calculation searches the moderator continuum for
values at which a pointwise confidence interval for a conditional slope
touches zero, and it labels the values on one side of those boundaries a
**region of significance** [@johnson1936; @bauer2005; @hayes2022]. It can
complement pick-a-point probes when the moderator is genuinely continuous
and no small set of theory-based values captures the question. It
replaces neither the conditional-slope curve, the magnitude estimates,
nor the support audit.

For this fitted curve the pointwise interval excludes zero below baseline
39.039 and above 51.284; between these values it covers zero. Appendix A
shows how the boundary equation and its sign determine those regions.
The figure lets us check what those numbers mean before interpreting them.

This example reveals a support
limitation that a pair of printed roots would conceal. The lower boundary,
39.039, lies below the smallest generated
baseline score, 42.8747, so
0 of the 320 simulated
students fall in the “significantly negative” region: it exists in the
algebra and nowhere in the data. The upper boundary,
51.284, does lie inside the observed range, and
313 students
(97.8125 percent
of the sample) sit above it. The supported reading is therefore
one-sided: across almost the entire baseline range these data cover, the
practice slope is positive and separated from zero, and only a thin
low-baseline sliver of
7 students falls in the
interval-covers-zero region.

Any boundary is descriptive of that fitted model and its pointwise
procedure. Scanning many moderator values raises multiplicity questions;
a pointwise band is not a simultaneous band. A root outside the observed
range has no empirical support, and a root inside a sparse tail may still
be unstable. The phrase “region of significance” can also distract from
magnitude and uncertainty. Pick-a-point answers questions at chosen
values; Johnson-Neyman locates model-based zero-crossing boundaries.
Neither method discovers a uniquely correct moderator cutoff, protects
against specification search, or supplies simultaneous error control
[@preacher2006].


A **simultaneous band** answers a wider question: does one band cover the
entire conditional-slope curve? Under the correctly specified linear model
with independent Normal errors of constant variance, a Scheffé band for
the two coefficients determining that curve replaces 1.9675 by
$\sqrt{2F_{.95;2,316}}=2.4594$ in the estimate-plus-or-minus-SE calculation.
It is wider because its coverage applies jointly to every linear
combination of those two coefficients, hence every conditional slope.
The two counts the dimensions of this slope family, not all four
coefficients in the fitted mean model. Showing only the supported range
makes the display useful; it does not validate extrapolation. Section 6.4
compares this band with pointwise intervals from two calculations.


## Continuous by Categorical: Rank-Specific Slopes {#ch10-salary}


### The question, the records and the analysis sample

The sustained empirical question is:

> Among the faculty of this college in 2008-09, how does the linear
> association between years of service and mean nine-month salary differ
> across the assistant, associate, and full professor ranks?

Each row is one faculty member. The outcome is nine-month salary,
rescaled to thousands of dollars. The focal continuous predictor is
years of service at the institution. Rank is a three-level categorical
predictor. The target is a rank-conditional descriptive association and
conditional mean prediction within observed support. It is not a return
to loyalty, a promotion effect, or a claim about faculty salaries in
general.

::: {.callout-note title="Data and software source"}

The `Salaries` data are called directly from the
[`carData` package](https://cran.r-project.org/package=carData)
([package DOI](https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.carData)), which
documents them as the 2008-09 nine-month salaries of the assistant,
associate, and full professors at one U.S. college, collected as part of
the administration's ongoing monitoring of salary differences between
male and female faculty [@carData2022; @fox2019]. This chapter uses only
the package-distributed data and does not copy a local data file. One college
in one year is not a probability sample of academia, so all inferential
language below is bounded to these faculty under the working model.

Conditional trends are computed with the official
[`emmeans` package](https://rvlenth.github.io/emmeans/), whose
`emtrends()` function evaluates fitted slopes from a model reference
grid. The chapter also verifies key calculations from the fitted
coefficient vector and covariance matrix.
:::

The package dataset has 397 rows. The analysis rule is fixed before
model fitting: retain a row only when salary, years of service, and rank
are all observed, and use exactly the same rows for the additive and
interaction models. Completeness is verified rather than assumed.


The fixed analytic sample contains 397 faculty members:
67 assistant professors,
64 associate professors, and
266 full professors. Here the
complete-case rule excludes nothing, but stating and checking it is
still part of a prespecified analysis: the audit is what shows the rule
to be harmless rather than an untested assumption.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
d0 <- carData::Salaries
dat <- d0[complete.cases(d0[c("salary", "yrs.service", "rank")]), ]
dat$rank <- droplevels(dat$rank)
dat$salary_k <- dat$salary/1000
dat$service_c <- dat$yrs.service - 5
```
:::

### The centered model and its two product columns

The model centers years of service at 5:

$$
S_c=S-5.
$$

This anchor lies in the observed range of all three ranks — it is inside
even the narrow assistant-professor window. It is chosen so that rank
lower-order coefficients represent salary differences at a supported
common service value. It is not chosen to force a desired p-value or to
make the ranks comparable in every other respect.

With assistant professor as the reference level, the model is

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(Y\mid S_c,R)={}&\beta_0+\beta_SS_c
 +\beta_A I(R=\text{AssocProf})\\
&+\beta_P I(R=\text{Prof})
 +\beta_{SA}S_c I(R=\text{AssocProf})\\
&+\beta_{SP}S_c I(R=\text{Prof}).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-salary-interaction}

The three lines have the following interpretations:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Assistant:}&\beta_0+\beta_SS_c,\\
\text{Associate:}&(\beta_0+\beta_A)+(\beta_S+\beta_{SA})S_c,\\
\text{Professor:}&(\beta_0+\beta_P)+(\beta_S+\beta_{SP})S_c.
\end{array}
$$

The two product coefficients are slope differences from the assistant
rank. They are not the associate and full-professor slopes themselves.

### The two-degree-of-freedom product block

Because rank has three levels, its interaction with one continuous
predictor contributes two columns. The appropriate nested comparison
tests them jointly, and this omnibus block question comes before any
examination of individual slopes or their pairwise differences.


| Variance procedure | Numerator df | Denominator df | $F$ | $p$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Classical nested-model $F$ | 2 | 391 | 0.4860 | .6155 |
| Approximate HC3 joint Wald $F$ | 2 | 391 | 1.3138 | .2700 |

: Classical and approximate robust tests of the two-column service-by-rank product block. {#tbl-ch10-blocks tbl-colwidths="[40,16,18,13,13]"}


The block comparison gives
$F(2, 391)=
0.486$,
$p=.6155$. Under the linear-model working
assumptions, the data provide no clear evidence against one common
service slope for the three ranks. That is a statement about what these
data can distinguish, not a demonstration that the three slopes are
equal — the later interval estimates show how wide a range of slope
differences remains compatible. The test also does not say whether the
lines are exactly linear or whether rank causally changes the salary
return to service.

An approximate joint Wald sensitivity check using the HC3 covariance matrix — the
estimator named in the chapter box, which keeps the ordinary least
squares (OLS) coefficients that minimize the residual sum of squares but
rebuilds their covariance from leverage-adjusted squared residuals
instead of one pooled variance [@long2000] — gives
$F(2,
391)=
1.3138$,
$p=.27$. Dividing the robust Wald statistic by
the number of restrictions and comparing it with an $F$ distribution using
the residual degrees of freedom is a transparent finite-sample approximation,
not an exact robust $F$ reference result. The robust and classical block
procedures therefore support the same bounded conclusion here, although
the p-values differ because the procedures use different variance models,
not because the fitted slopes changed.

The order of `anova(reduced, full)` matters for readable output and for
the narrative. Both models must use the same response and exactly the
same rows. If the full model silently loses more observations because a
new variable is missing, the models are not nested on a common dataset
and the comparison no longer answers the intended block question. Here
the analysis sample was fixed once, before fitting, so the printed row
counts agree by construction.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
s0 <- lm(salary_k ~ service_c + rank, data = dat)
anova(s0, s1)
```
:::

## Factor by Factor: Cell Means Revisited {#ch10-cells}


### Two factors: the same nonadditive question

When both predictors are factors, an interaction is nonadditivity among
cell means. The `carData::Moore` data provide a compact
illustration from social psychology: 45 participants in a conformity
experiment [@moore1971], with the number of conforming
responses as the outcome, the manipulated status of a partner (low or
high) as one factor, and the participant's measured authoritarianism
category (low, medium, or high F-scale score) as a three-level factor.
The package documentation describes partner status as manipulated but
does not document random assignment or the full experimental protocol;
the example therefore treats it as an experimental-condition contrast
rather than assuming causal identification from the dataset description
alone.
This example is separate from the salary analysis and is not needed for
its conclusions. Under the classical common-variance linear model, its
product block is statistically detectable; the conclusion is sensitive
to the variance model and outcome scale, as shown below. The cell
summary reports, for each of the six cells, its size, its mean number of
conforming responses, and its standard deviation (SD), the typical
distance of a participant's score from that cell's mean.

### The block, simple differences and interaction contrast

The block has two degrees of freedom because a three-level
authoritarianism factor contributes two indicator columns and therefore
two product columns. No middle category is discarded to manufacture a
2-by-2 table. The classical test gives
$F(2, 39)=
4.1846$,
$p=.0226$, whereas the approximate HC3
joint Wald test gives $F(2,
39)=
2.8294$,
$p=.0712$. The cells are small and unbalanced,
their spreads differ, and conformity is a bounded count. Ordinary linear
model inference is therefore a working approximation here, not a
scale-robust verdict. The cell-mean pattern remains pedagogically useful;
the strength of inferential evidence must be reported as
variance-model-sensitive.

For any two authoritarianism categories, a **statistical
difference-in-differences (DiD)** — the difference between two group
differences — is an interaction contrast. Comparing the low and high
categories gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat C_{\mathrm{DD}}={}&(\bar y_{\text{low},H}-\bar y_{\text{low},L})\\
&-(\bar y_{\text{high},H}-\bar y_{\text{high},L}),
\end{aligned}
$$

where $H$ and $L$ denote high- and low-status partners.


The contrast is 9.2679 conforming responses: the
partner-status difference is about
8.5
responses among low-authoritarianism participants and about
$-0.7679$
among high-authoritarianism participants. Algebraically it is a
product-term contrast. Partner status is described as manipulated, but
the package documentation alone does not establish random assignment,
implementation fidelity, or the absence of post-assignment complications.
The status comparison should therefore be described as an
experimental-condition contrast unless the original study documentation
supplies those warrants. Authoritarianism is measured rather than
assigned, so any variation of the status contrast across F-scale
categories also depends on observational group comparability. In a policy
or before-after study, a causal difference-in-differences
interpretation would additionally require a defensible treatment and
timing design, a counterfactual trend argument such as parallel trends,
absence of relevant anticipatory or spillover behavior, and uncertainty
appropriate to the assignment and dependence structure. Those
design-based methods are outside this chapter.

### What the difference of differences does not carry

::: {.callout-warning title="Statistical interaction is not a causal design"}

A product term describes nonadditivity in a model. Causal interpretation
comes from design and assumptions outside the coefficient algebra. The
same product term can appear in an observational cross-section, a
randomized factorial experiment, or a longitudinal policy comparison;
those settings do not inherit the same causal meaning.
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
moore <- carData::Moore
with(moore, tapply(conformity, list(fcategory, partner.status), mean))
c1 <- lm(conformity ~ partner.status * fcategory, data = moore)
```
:::


For low versus high authoritarianism, the interaction contrast is

$$
\widehat C_{\mathrm{DD}}
=(\bar y_{\mathrm{low},H}-\bar y_{\mathrm{low},L})
-(\bar y_{\mathrm{high},H}-\bar y_{\mathrm{high},L})
=\mathbf c{}^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=9.2679,
\qquad SE=\sqrt{\mathbf c{}^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf c}=3.4507.
$$

The classical pointwise interval is [2.2883, 16.2475]. If this comparison
was selected after inspecting the cell pattern, the comparison family
needs a simultaneous calibration as in Chapter 4; an attractive contrast
is not retroactively prespecified.

## Check, Qualify and Resample {#ch10-checks}


### Where the model is likely to strain

The salary interaction model assumes an adequately linear conditional
mean within each rank, independent information from the modeled rows,
and sufficient joint service-by-rank support. Classical standard errors
and prediction intervals additionally use a common residual variance;
small-sample exact $t$ and $F$ results use a conditional Normal-error
model. Leverage and influence matter because product columns can make
sparse predictor combinations especially consequential. Residual plots
do not certify these assumptions; they show where parts of the
approximation may be incomplete [@fox2016; @gelman2020].



::: {.cell}

The HC3 standard errors introduced with the block test replace the
common-variance coefficient covariance matrix with a leverage-adjusted,
residual-based estimate while retaining the OLS coefficients and the
fitted mean model [@long2000; @zeileis2004]. Standard errors, approximate
intervals, and approximate joint Wald tests derived from that matrix can
change. Applied to the rank-specific trends, they are a sensitivity analysis
for uncertainty, not a repair for a wrong conditional mean and not a license
to ignore dependence.

associate-professor slope excludes zero
while the classical interval does not. A borderline conclusion that
moves when the variance model changes should be reported as sensitive,
not resolved by quietly choosing whichever calculation looks better.
There is a second trap here. Under HC3 the associate slope interval
excludes zero and the full-professor interval covers zero. That does not
show that the two slopes differ. Their directly estimated
associate-minus-full contrast is $-0.2754$, with approximate HC3 SE
0.2524 and interval [$-0.7716$, 0.2209] using the same residual-df
reference ($p=.2759$). The interval leaves substantial uncertainty about
the direction of the slope difference. Comparing two labels discards the
very covariance that the contrast needs; its nonrejection also does not
establish equal slopes.

Neither calculation repairs the fitted mean, the design, or the
dependence structure.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

cvec <- c(0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0)  # associate slope
sqrt(drop(cvec %*% V %*% cvec))
```

### Influence and a competing explanation

The most influential row is a full professor with
60 years of service and a salary of
192.253 thousand dollars — a
long-service, high-leverage point at the far edge of the professor
range. Omitting it moves the professor slope slightly and leaves the
other slopes essentially unchanged; the largest Cook's distance is
small, and the broad pattern of imprecise, overlapping slopes remains.
This leave-one-out fit is a sensitivity description. Deletion would
require a documented recording error, an explicit target-population
rule, or another substantive reason independent of Cook's distance.

If the true relationship is curved and ranks occupy different ranges,
separate straight lines can appear to have different slopes even when
the same curved function applies. A compact sensitivity model adds one
common quadratic service term while retaining the full lower-order
interaction structure.


This one-degree-of-freedom check provides little evidence that a shared
quadratic term materially improves the fitted mean. It does not prove
that every rank relationship is exactly linear. Rank-specific curvature
would require additional terms and, for assistant professors,
substantially more support than a six-year window can offer. A
sensitivity model should clarify a plausible failure mode, not become an
unrestricted search for significance.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
which.max(cooks.distance(s1))
anova(s1, lm(salary_k ~ service_c * rank + I(service_c^2), dat))
```

## From Analysis to a Defensible Claim {#ch10-report}


### The pattern before the verdict

The interaction block answers whether one common slope is adequate under
the fitted linear model. A defensible report does not stop there. It
describes the conditional pattern, gives interval estimates in original
units, shows where the comparisons are supported, and states what the
design does not identify.

For the salary analysis, the main pieces are:

- 397 faculty members at one college in 2008-09, with
  rank-specific service ranges shown explicitly;
- a hierarchical model with salary in thousands of dollars, service
  centered at 5 years, and a two-degree-of-freedom product block;
- an omnibus interaction comparison of
  $F(2, 391)=
  0.486$,
  $p=.6155$;
- estimated within-rank slopes with confidence intervals;
- fitted means or contrasts at a supported common service value;
- residual, unequal-variance, influence, curvature, and support checks;
- three uncertainty procedures for the same conditional slopes, including
  the one slope whose approximate sensitivity interval excludes zero under
  HC3 and case resampling but not under the classical common-variance model;
  and
- an observational interpretation bounded to the represented data.

::: {.callout-tip title="A bounded report"}

Among the 397 faculty members of this college in
2008-09, rank differences in mean nine-month salary were large, but the
data provided no clear evidence that the linear service-salary
association differed across ranks
($F(2, 391)=
0.486$,
$p=.6155$). Within each rank's observed range,
the estimated slopes were
0.7793 thousand dollars per
service year for assistant professors
(95% confidence interval [$-3.045$,
4.6036]),
$-0.3947$ for associate
professors ([$-0.9744$,
0.185]), and
$-0.1193$ for full professors
([$-0.3656$,
0.127]). Every classical interval includes zero
and the intervals overlap; the assistant-professor slope rests on a
service range of only
0 to

associate-professor slope was the one quantity sensitive to the variance

to service, identify promotion or cohort mechanisms, or support
extrapolation beyond observed rank-service combinations.
:::

This paragraph reports a null block result without converting it into a
claim that the slopes are equal, and it reports the variance-model
sensitivity instead of quietly resolving it. Reporting what the data
cannot distinguish is as much a finding as reporting what they can.


### A reusable template and the statements it blocks

A reusable interaction report can be organized in six sentences.

1. **Target and unit:** “Among [analytic units], we examined whether the
   [outcome-unit] association between [focal predictor] and [outcome]
   varied across [moderator values or groups].”
2. **Model and support:** “We fit a hierarchical [model scale] model on
   [fixed sample], with probes restricted to [observed joint support].”
3. **Block evidence:** “Adding the [named] product block changed model fit
   by [degrees of freedom, statistic, interval or p-value].”
4. **Conditional estimates:** “At [prespecified supported values], the
   estimated slopes or contrasts were [estimates and intervals in units].”
5. **Checks:** “Residual, variance, influence, curvature, and alternative-
   coding checks suggested [specific consequences].”
6. **Boundary:** “The result supports [bounded associational or predictive
   conclusion] but does not establish [causality, mechanism,
   generalization, or unsupported extrapolation].”

Not every paper must use these exact sentences. Every report should make
their information recoverable.

| Attractive statement | Why it fails | Defensible replacement |
|:--|:--|:--|
| "The interaction proves moderation." | A product term is model-based nonadditivity; substantive moderation needs a theory-defined role and a design. | "The fitted conditional slope varied across the named values or groups." |
| "There is no effect of $X$." | The lower-order coefficient is the slope only at the coded zero or reference value. | "At $W=0$ under this coding the estimated slope of $X$ was ..." |
| "The lines interact only if they cross." | Interaction means nonparallelism on the modelled scale. | "The estimated slopes differed over the displayed support." |
| "Centering fixed the collinearity and the confounding." | Centering changes the origin, not the information, the omitted variables, or the design. | "Centering made the zero-value comparison interpretable." |
| "The product $p$-value shows where the effect exists." | One block test does not describe conditional magnitudes across the moderator. | "The slope curve with its band and support shows where the comparison is estimated and how precisely." |
| "One group's slope is significant and another's is not, so they differ." | Two significance verdicts are not a test of their difference. | "The slope contrast was ... with interval ..." |
| "A large product $p$-value shows the slopes are equal." | Nonrejection is not evidence of no difference. | "A slope difference between ... and ... remains compatible with these records; claims are restricted to observed joint support." |

: Common interaction overclaims and their defensible replacements. {#tbl-ch10-overclaims tbl-colwidths="[28,38,34]"}

The sustained salary example is exactly this situation, so it deserves
its own statement of principle. A large product p-value is not proof
that conditional slopes are exactly equal. It says the data and model do
not distinguish the product block from zero with the chosen precision
and reference procedure. A bounded null report gives the estimated
difference and its interval, then asks whether values of practical
importance remain compatible with the data.

For example, suppose an estimated slope difference is 0.08 outcome units
per predictor unit with a 95% interval from $-0.12$ to 0.28. “No
interaction” hides the fact that modest negative and positive differences
remain compatible. The relevant next question is substantive: would any
part of that interval change the decision or theory?

Why can a study estimate a large average association while leaving
moderation imprecise? A product coefficient needs information about how
comparisons vary across **joint predictor combinations**. Consider the
same 320 generated students. Keep practice hours and each student's
original generated error fixed, compress the centered baseline scores
to 30% of their original deviations, and generate scores again from the
same equation, including the true product coefficient 0.12. This changes
the design's predictor coverage, not the true interaction or error SD.

## Reading Bridge

A product term releases a common-slope restriction. Lower-order
coefficients are comparisons at stated anchors; centering and releveling
move the coordinates without changing the fitted surface. Conditional
slopes, group contrasts and differences of differences all use coefficient
covariance for their uncertainty. The block test examines additivity;
curves, intervals and support show what the comparison means.

The salary records illustrated an honest weak-interaction result and one
slope sensitive to the variance assumption. Chapter 11 changes the outcome
to binary and the mean scale to the logit. The conditional question
continues, but interaction on the linear-predictor and probability scales
will become different statements about the same fit.

### Key terms {.unnumbered}

| Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction |
|:--|:--|
| Product term (interaction term; multiplicative term) | A column formed by multiplying two predictors, so that each one's fitted comparison depends on the other's value. Its coefficient is a difference in slopes, not a slope, and nonadditivity is defined on the modelled scale: a nonlinear change of outcome scale can create or remove it. |
| Conditional slope (simple slope; conditional effect) | The fitted difference in outcome per one-unit difference in a focal predictor evaluated at a stated value or group of the other predictor. It is a linear combination of coefficients, so its SE uses their covariance, and it describes a conditional mean, not an individual case. |
| Moderator (moderating variable; moderation) | The variable across whose values or groups a named focal relationship is allowed to vary. The product-term algebra is symmetric in the two predictors, so the label comes from the research question; a moderation reading describes when a relationship differs, not how an effect is transmitted. |
| Hierarchy principle (marginality; well-formulated model) | The rule that a model containing a product also contains both component terms. Dropping a component forces the other's slope to zero at its coded zero and makes the fitted surface depend on the origin; hierarchy does not require that every possible product be added. |
| Centering a predictor (anchoring; reparameterization) | Replacing a predictor by its difference from a chosen value, so that coefficients anchored at zero become comparisons at that value. It changes the intercept and the lower-order coefficients and leaves the product coefficient, the fitted values, the residuals and the product-block test unchanged; it repairs no design, selection, or measurement problem. |
| Probe value (pick-a-point value) | A stated value of the moderator at which a conditional slope or contrast is evaluated, chosen from the measurement scale, a threshold, or a decision need rather than by an automatic mean-and-SD rule, and restricted to values the records support. |
| Johnson--Neyman boundary (region of significance) | A moderator value at which a pointwise interval for a conditional slope touches zero, found as a root of a quadratic whose leading coefficient decides which side is the region. A boundary outside the observed support describes the algebra and not the data, and a pointwise band is not a simultaneous band. |
| Interaction contrast (difference in differences within a model) | A linear combination of coefficients comparing two conditional comparisons, such as one group's difference minus another group's difference. Under reference coding it equals a product coefficient up to sign; its SE uses the coefficient covariance, and its causal reading depends on design, not on the algebra. |

## Appendix A: Conditional quantities as linear combinations {.unnumbered}

### One formula for four questions {.unnumbered}

A conditional slope, conditional mean, group contrast and interaction
contrast can all be written $\mathbf c{}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta$. The vector $\mathbf c$ names the
question; the estimated variance is $\mathbf c{}^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf c$. For coefficient order
$(\beta_0,\beta_X,\beta_W,\beta_{XW})$:

| Quantity | Contrast vector $\mathbf c{}^{\mathsf T}$ |
|:--|:--|
| Practice slope at $w$ | $(0,1,0,w)$ |
| Mean at $(x,w)$ | $(1,x,w,xw)$ |
| Mean difference $x_b-x_a$ at $w$ | $(0,x_b-x_a,0,w(x_b-x_a))$ |
| Slope difference at $w_b$ and $w_a$ | $(0,0,0,w_b-w_a)$ |

: Different questions use the same coefficient covariance. {#tbl-ch10-linear tbl-colwidths="[50,50]"}

At $w=10$ the first row gives 3.8461 with SE 0.1947 from full precision.
The faculty associate slope uses $\mathbf c{}^{\mathsf T}=(0,1,0,0,1,0)$ and gives $-0.3947$
with classical SE 0.2949. The uncertainty belongs to the whole comparison,
not a sum of separate coefficient SEs.

### Centering translates the coefficients {.unnumbered}

For $W_c=W-c$,

$$
\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathrm{new}}=\mathbf T\boldsymbol\beta,
\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&c&0\\0&1&0&c\\0&0&1&0\\0&0&0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \mathbf V^{\mathrm{new}}=\mathbf T\mathbf V\mathbf T{}^{\mathsf T}.
$$

The last row fixes the product coefficient. The first two translate the
anchor. With $c=70$, the full-precision raw estimates give intercept
59.6123 and practice coefficient 2.6972. A translated contrast uses the
translated covariance; its estimate and SE then agree with the original.

### The boundary quadratic {.unnumbered}

Writing $a=\widehat\beta_X$, $b=\widehat\beta_{XW}$,
$v_a=\widehat{\mathbf V}_{XX}$, $v_b=\widehat{\mathbf V}_{XW,XW}$ and
$v_{ab}=\widehat{\mathbf V}_{X,XW}$, the squared endpoint condition becomes

$$
Aw^2+Bw+C=0,\quad A=b^2-t^2v_b,\quad
B=2ab-2t^2v_{ab},\quad C=a^2-t^2v_a.
$$

For distinct real roots, the band excludes zero outside them if $A>0$
and inside if $A<0$. With $A=0$ the condition is linear; with no real
roots the sign is constant and must be checked at a supported value.
The generated fit has $A=0.0125$ and baseline roots 39.039 and 51.284.
Substitution into the quadratic gives numerical zero, and the pointwise
interval touches zero there. The lower root remains outside the data.

## Appendix B: What changes beyond this chapter {.unnumbered}

A three-way product $XWZ$ allows a two-way pattern to vary with a third
predictor. Hierarchy keeps all two-way products and all component terms.
Its interpretation requires conditional comparisons across three dimensions;
Chapter 4's three-way table gives the categorical reading.

With a nonlinear link, additivity on the linear-predictor scale and on
the response scale are different properties. Even without a product, a
logistic model can give probability differences that vary with another
predictor. Always name the scale.

A conditional indirect effect concerns mediation. Its causal interpretation
needs defensible temporal ordering, adequate functional form and assumptions
about common causes of the intervening variable and outcome. An interval
around an unidentified causal quantity leaves that problem in place.

Department, classroom or school dependence changes the appropriate
uncertainty calculation. Adding a product changes a conditional mean;
it does not make records independent.
